title: Can you sell a house with foundation problems
description: Can you sell a house with foundation problems? Yes, if the price and the disclosure match what you know. A repair is a choice, not a ban.
summary: A foundation problem does not by itself stop a sale. Silence about a problem you know is the part that fails.
body: Can you sell a house with foundation problems? Yes. Buyers purchase houses that need piers, drainage, or monitoring when the report and the price are in the file. What you cannot sell is a story that the floors are fine when you have a letter that says they are not. This is not an engineering opinion and it is not legal advice. Your state's disclosure form is the legal piece. The foundation guide is the order of checks.

Write what you can point at before you hire anyone: doors that newly stick, a crack that grew, a slope you can feel. A stable hairline you have watched for years is a different line. If the list is more than that hairline, get a written letter from a structural engineer and a bid that names a scope. A salesperson's visit is not that letter. A typical range for an engineer's letter is often a few hundred dollars to around a thousand. The invoice is the number that counts.

Then choose repair, credit, or sell with the report disclosed. [Selling a house as is vs fixing up](/tips/selling-as-is-vs-fixing-up) is the short choice. As-is still means you tell the truth. Put the bid or the credit into the net calculator before you publish a price. A buyer can still walk, inspect, and ask for more. Your job is to make the first conversation match the house.

If you are in Texas, the Texas disclosure note points at the TREC form and Section 5.008 as that form describes it. Other states have their own forms. Do not copy a Texas answer onto another state's blank. Ask a local lawyer if you are unsure the question applies.
steps: Write the symptoms you can point at and whether they have changed.
Get an engineer's letter if the movement is new or growing.
Price a repair bid or a credit before you list.
Disclose the reports you have. Do not wait for the buyer's inspector.
Use your state's form, not a form from somewhere else.

title: Do you have to disclose foundation issues
description: Do you have to disclose foundation issues you know about? State forms ask about known defects. In Texas, start with the TREC seller disclosure.
summary: If you know about a foundation problem or a report, the disclosure form is where it goes. Hiding it is not a pricing strategy.
body: Do you have to disclose foundation issues? If you know about them, the honest answer on a seller disclosure is yes, in the way that form asks. This is not legal advice. The form and the statute control, and they vary. In Texas, the [TREC Seller's Disclosure Notice](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/sellers-disclosure-notice) says it contains information required by Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code about material facts and the physical condition of the property. Read the instructions before you decide your sale is exempt.

Known means a report in a drawer, a repair you paid for, a crack you watched widen, or a contractor who told you the corner was moving. It does not mean you must diagnose every hairline like an engineer. If you do not know, say what you see or get a letter. Answering no because you hope the buyer's inspector is rushed is how a later claim starts. Filling a crack the week before the visit and then forgetting the fill is the same problem.

Give the whole report if you give any of it. A summary you wrote is not a substitute for the letter you have. When the buyer asks for a repair, answer with a scope and a payer in the contract. [Repair requests after inspection](/tips/ask-who-pays-for-requested-repairs) is that habit. Foundation is not a special exception to writing things down.

A warranty does not replace the form. A warranty is a product with exclusions. Disclosure is what you knew. You can offer both. You cannot offer the warranty instead of the truth. Put the form in the closing folder with the report so the answer you gave is the answer you can find later. If a second report arrives, add it to the same folder instead of starting a new story.
steps: Read the disclosure form your state actually uses.
List reports, prior repairs, and symptoms you have seen.
Answer from that list. Do not answer from optimism.
If you are unsure the form applies, ask a local lawyer.
Attach the report instead of paraphrasing the pages you like.

title: How to sell a house with foundation problems
description: How to sell a house with foundation problems: document the issue, choose repair or credit, price the net, and disclose the report before you list.
summary: Pick repair, a credit, or an as-is sale with the report attached, and make the list price match that choice.
body: How to sell a house with foundation problems is a sequence. See it, write it, price it, disclose it, then negotiate it. Skip a step and the buyer's inspector becomes the first person to name the crack, on a deadline. The foundation guide is the longer version. This note is the sale path after you already have a list of symptoms.

Get two numbers on the same scope if you might repair: an engineer's description and a contractor's bid. A typical range for a repair can run from a few thousand dollars for a limited area to much more for a whole side. Do not publish a national price as your cost. Type the bid you would actually sign into the [net proceeds calculator](/tools/net-proceeds). If you will not repair, decide the credit you would offer and type that instead. [Home pricing strategy](/tips/write-three-numbers-before-you-list) still wants a bottom line.

Photos should match the disclosure. Do not crop out the corner you just described in writing. The listing-photo guide says to show repairs you finished and not to pretend. If the work is scheduled but not done, say so. A buyer who sees the report and the corner in the same afternoon is a buyer you can negotiate with. A buyer who feels tricked will use the repair request to leave.

When the offer arrives, compare net and dates the way the offers guide says. A higher price that demands a full repair you will not manage can be worse than a lower price that accepts the report. Counter in writing. Do not agree to make it right without a drawing and a dollar limit. Keep the bid and the disclosure in the same folder as the offers so the counter uses the same crack.
steps: Attach the report and the bid to your pricing sheet.
Choose repair, credit, or as-is with disclosure, and write it down.
Set the list price from the net that includes that choice.
Photograph the house you disclosed.
Answer repair demands with a scope, a cap, and a signature.

title: Foundation issues in Texas
description: Foundation issues in Texas still go on the TREC seller disclosure when you know about them. The form cites Property Code section 5.008. Not legal advice.
summary: Texas sellers use the TREC notice for known foundation facts. Movement in the soil does not create a special silence.
body: This is not legal advice. Foundation issues in Texas are common enough that people treat cracks as small talk. The disclosure is not small talk. The [TREC Seller's Disclosure Notice](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/sellers-disclosure-notice) says it is for sellers of previously occupied single-family residences and that it includes information required by Section 5.008 of the Texas Property Code about material facts and physical condition. Read the form's questions about foundations, repairs, and water. Answer from what you know.

Soil that shrinks and swells is a reason to look, not a reason to skip the form. Write prior pier work, warranties, and engineer's letters. If a company installed piers, you should have an invoice or a transferable warranty. Find it before a buyer asks. If you never had a letter and you only see a hairline, say what you see. Do not write none because every house on the block has a crack.

A repair bid in your city is the cost that belongs on the net sheet. A typical range is only a label: limited work can be a few thousand dollars, and a larger scope costs more. Get the scope in writing. The Texas seller guide on this site covers the rest of the checklist, including the option period. A buyer can inspect and terminate under the contract you sign. Disclosure does not remove that right. It removes the surprise.

If the house is in an estate or a trust, you still need authority to sign the notice and the deed. The inherited-house guide is that step. An heir who fills out the disclosure from childhood memory should say what they personally know and what they do not. Guessing no is not a kindness to the other heirs.
steps: Read the foundation questions on the current TREC seller disclosure.
Gather old pier invoices, warranties, and engineer letters.
Answer from those papers and from what you have seen.
Put any repair bid on the net sheet before you list.
Ask a Texas lawyer if you do not know whether the notice applies.
